Local Optimality Conditions

Reference Section 4.2 in Biegler (2010)

Unconstrained comparison¶

For twice continuously differentiable objectives, a local unconstrained minimum has zero gradient and positive-semidefinite Hessian. These are necessary conditions; they do not classify every stationary point. The definitions, derivative tests and proofs have their existing home in Unconstrained Optimality Conditions. Here the feasible neighborhood and constraint reactions change the test.

Balance of Forces Interpretation¶

Here is a helpful handout.

Consider min⁡f(x)\min f(\mathbf{x})minf(x) subject to g(x)≤0g(\mathbf{x})\le0g(x)≤0. The objective is a landscape; its downhill force is −∇f-\nabla f−∇f. The fence force is −u∇g-u\nabla g−u∇g, with u≥0u\ge0u≥0, pointing toward the feasible side.

The drawn arrows are gradients, pointing toward increasing values. At a regular constrained minimum with an active pushing fence,

∇f(x∗)+u∗∇g(x∗)=0.\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*)+u^*\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^*)=0.∇f(x∗)+u∗∇g(x∗)=0.
(1)

The objective contour is tangent to the fence. Opposite gradient directions do not require equal lengths: the multiplier supplies the scale. Rescaling a constraint changes the numerical multiplier, so raw arrow lengths are not force magnitudes.

Source: Biegler (2010), Figures 4.5–4.6, pp.68–69. The handout and website use this same prepared drawing.

An equality h(x)=0h(\mathbf{x})=0h(x)=0 acts as a rail. Its force −v∇h-v\nabla h−v∇h can point either way, because vvv is unrestricted.

Balance is ∇f+u∇g+v∇h=0\nabla f+u\nabla g+v\nabla h=0∇f+u∇g+v∇h=0. For this illustrative drawing the normalized gradients are approximately

∇f=(0.9825,0.1861)T,∇g=(−0.8587,−0.5125)T,∇h=(−0.8480,0.5300)T.\nabla f=(0.9825,0.1861)^T,\quad \nabla g=(-0.8587,-0.5125)^T,\quad \nabla h=(-0.8480,0.5300)^T.∇f=(0.9825,0.1861)T,∇g=(−0.8587,−0.5125)T,∇h=(−0.8480,0.5300)T.
(2)

They give u≈0.76265>0u\approx0.76265>0u≈0.76265>0, v≈0.38634v\approx0.38634v≈0.38634. For a trial direction p\mathbf pp, a small positive step is x∗+αp\mathbf x^*+\alpha\mathbf px∗+αp. Differentiability gives ϕ(x∗+αp)=ϕ(x∗)+α∇ϕ(x∗)Tp+o(α)\phi(\mathbf x^*+\alpha\mathbf p)=\phi(\mathbf x^*)+\alpha\nabla\phi(\mathbf x^*)^T\mathbf p+o(\alpha)ϕ(x∗+αp)=ϕ(x∗)+α∇ϕ(x∗)Tp+o(α) for ϕ=f,g,h\phi=f,g,hϕ=f,g,h. A direction is linearized-feasible when every equality derivative is zero and every active inequality derivative is nonpositive. The direction p=(0.5300,0.8480)T\mathbf p=(0.5300,0.8480)^Tp=(0.5300,0.8480)T is tangent to the rail, enters the feasible side of the fence, and raises the objective to first order. Its negative crosses the fence. Thus there is feasible motion, but no nonzero critical direction at this intersection. “No allowable directions” in a curvature discussion refers to the critical cone, not all feasible motion.

For the displayed rounded vectors, the equality tangent space is one-dimensional: every tangent vector is p=t(0.5300,0.8480)T\mathbf p=t(0.5300,0.8480)^Tp=t(0.5300,0.8480)T, t∈Rt\in\mathbb Rt∈R. The exact dot products of these supplied decimals are

∇hTp=0,∇gTp=−0.889711t,∇fTp=0.6785378t.\nabla h^T\mathbf p=0,\qquad \nabla g^T\mathbf p=-0.889711t,\qquad \nabla f^T\mathbf p=0.6785378t.∇hTp=0,∇gTp=−0.889711t,∇fTp=0.6785378t.
(3)

The linearized inequality therefore requires t≥0t\ge0t≥0, and zero first-order objective change then requires t=0t=0t=0. This establishes the whole critical cone {0}\{0\}{0} rather than testing only one direction. These conclusions describe the prepared drawing; the derivatives of the later log-model are calculated independently.

Removing the rail permits a downhill direction along the fence toward its tangency minimum. For example, q=(−0.5125,0.8587)T\mathbf q=(-0.5125,0.8587)^Tq=(−0.5125,0.8587)T has ∇gTq=0\nabla g^T\mathbf q=0∇gTq=0 and ∇fTq=−0.34372718<0\nabla f^T\mathbf q=-0.34372718<0∇fTq=−0.34372718<0. But ∇hTq=0.889711≠0\nabla h^T\mathbf q=0.889711\ne0∇hTq=0.889711=0, so the rail excludes this descent direction. Source: Biegler (2010), Figure 4.7 and Eq. (4.9), pp.70–71. The later numerical example uses its own objective and gradients; these normalized drawing vectors are not substituted into that model.

Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) necessary conditions¶

At a feasible candidate x∗\mathbf x^*x∗, inequality iii is active when gi(x∗)=0g_i(\mathbf x^*)=0gi​(x∗)=0 and inactive when gi(x∗)<0g_i(\mathbf x^*)<0gi​(x∗)<0. Define row-oriented Jacobians by

[Jg(x)]i,:=∇xgi(x)T,[Jh(x)]j,:=∇xhj(x)T,[\mathbf J_g(\mathbf x)]_{i,:}=\nabla_{\mathbf x}g_i(\mathbf x)^T,\qquad [\mathbf J_h(\mathbf x)]_{j,:}=\nabla_{\mathbf x}h_j(\mathbf x)^T,[Jg​(x)]i,:​=∇x​gi​(x)T,[Jh​(x)]j,:​=∇x​hj​(x)T,
(4)

so Jg∈Rr×n\mathbf J_g\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}Jg​∈Rr×n and Jh∈Rm×n\mathbf J_h\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}Jh​∈Rm×n. Use

L(x,u,v)=f(x)+g(x)Tu+h(x)Tv.\mathcal L(\mathbf x,\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=f(\mathbf x)+ \mathbf g(\mathbf x)^T\mathbf u+\mathbf h(\mathbf x)^T\mathbf v.L(x,u,v)=f(x)+g(x)Tu+h(x)Tv.
(5)

Assume fff, all gig_igi​, and all hjh_jhj​ are continuously differentiable (C1C^1C1) on an open neighborhood of a feasible local minimum. The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) means the combined indexed family (∇xgi(x∗))i:gi(x∗)=0(\nabla_{\mathbf x}g_i(\mathbf x^*))_{i:g_i(\mathbf x^*)=0}(∇x​gi​(x∗))i:gi​(x∗)=0​ and (∇xhj(x∗))j=1m(\nabla_{\mathbf x}h_j(\mathbf x^*))_{j=1}^m(∇x​hj​(x∗))j=1m​ is linearly independent. If LICQ holds there, the following necessary multiplier conditions apply:

∇xL=∇f+JgTu+JhTv=0,g≤0,h=0,u≥0,giui=0for every i.\begin{aligned} \nabla_{\mathbf x}\mathcal L&=\nabla f+\mathbf J_g^T\mathbf u+\mathbf J_h^T\mathbf v=0,\\ \mathbf g&\le0,\qquad\mathbf h=0,\qquad\mathbf u\ge0,\\ g_i u_i&=0\quad\text{for every }i. \end{aligned}∇x​Lggi​ui​​=∇f+JgT​u+JhT​v=0,≤0,h=0,u≥0,=0for every i.​
(6)

Evaluate these at the candidate. Equality multipliers have no sign restriction. Dot-product complementarity gTu=0\mathbf g^T\mathbf u=0gTu=0 is equivalent to the component conditions because every summand is nonpositive. The prepared product-vector diagram compares nonpositive terms with a zero vector. If any term is strictly negative, no other nonpositive term can cancel it to make the sum zero.

Inactive constraints have gi<0g_i<0gi​<0, hence ui=0u_i=0ui​=0. Active constraints have gi=0g_i=0gi​=0 and may have a positive multiplier (strongly active) or zero multiplier (weakly active).

Regularity is a hypothesis. LICQ means the equality gradients and active inequality gradients are linearly independent. It is one sufficient qualification for the first-order necessary conditions. For min⁡x\min xminx subject to x2=0x^2=0x2=0, the only feasible point is a strict global minimum, but 1+v(2x)=01+v(2x)=01+v(2x)=0 cannot hold at zero for any multiplier. The constraint gradient is zero. See Constraint Qualifications for the full theory.

Feasible and critical directions differ. The linearized feasible cone imposes Jhp=0\mathbf J_h\mathbf p=0Jh​p=0 and ∇giTp≤0\nabla g_i^T\mathbf p\le0∇giT​p≤0 on active inequalities. At a KKT point,

∇fTp=−∑iui∇giTp≥0.\nabla f^T\mathbf p=-\sum_iu_i\nabla g_i^T\mathbf p\ge0.∇fTp=−i∑​ui​∇giT​p≥0.
(7)

Critical directions have zero first-order objective change. Since every term on the right is nonnegative, they are exactly the directions satisfying

Jhp=0,∇giTp=0gi=0, ui>0,∇giTp≤0gi=0, ui=0.\begin{aligned} \mathbf J_h\mathbf p&=0,\\ \nabla g_i^T\mathbf p&=0&&g_i=0,\ u_i>0,\\ \nabla g_i^T\mathbf p&\le0&&g_i=0,\ u_i=0. \end{aligned}Jh​p∇giT​p∇giT​p​=0,=0≤0​​gi​=0, ui​>0,gi​=0, ui​=0.​
(8)

A positive multiplier does not prevent every feasible inward move; it makes that move raise the objective to first order. Such a direction is not critical. These are first-order tangent tests; nonlinear constraints need not remain feasible along an entire straight step.

For g=−x2g=-x_2g=−x2​ at the origin, f=x12+x2f=x_1^2+x_2f=x12​+x2​ has u=1u=1u=1 and critical directions p2=0p_2=0p2​=0. Its feasible directions with p2>0p_2>0p2​>0 already raise the objective. For f=x12+x22f=x_1^2+x_2^2f=x12​+x22​, u=0u=0u=0 and every linearized feasible direction p2≥0p_2\ge0p2​≥0 is critical.

With fff, every gig_igi​, and every hjh_jhj​ twice continuously differentiable (C2C^2C2) on an open neighborhood and LICQ at a local minimum, second-order necessity gives

pT∇xx2L p≥0for every critical direction p.\mathbf p^T\nabla_{\mathbf{xx}}^2\mathcal L\,\mathbf p\ge0 \quad\text{for every critical direction }\mathbf p.pT∇xx2​Lp≥0for every critical direction p.
(9)

Together with KKT, strict positivity on every nonzero critical direction is sufficient for a strict local minimum. The two examples satisfy it on their respective cones. If the critical cone is {0}\{0\}{0}, the strict condition is vacuous; feasible noncritical directions are controlled by their positive first-order change. Full theorem/proof material has its existing home in Second-Order Conditions.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Eqs. (4.9)–(4.12), pp.70–71; Theorems 4.14–4.15, pp.77–78; critical cone in §4.3.3, p.79; Theorems 4.17–4.18, pp.80–81. The constraint-qualification counterexample follows directly from its singleton feasible set and zero constraint derivative.

For these two quadratic examples, the distinction is exact. At the origin and for any positive α\alphaα,

f1(αp)−f1(0)=αp2+α2p12,f2(αp)−f2(0)=α2(p12+p22).\begin{aligned} f_1(\alpha\mathbf p)-f_1(0)&=\alpha p_2+\alpha^2p_1^2,\\ f_2(\alpha\mathbf p)-f_2(0)&=\alpha^2(p_1^2+p_2^2). \end{aligned}f1​(αp)−f1​(0)f2​(αp)−f2​(0)​=αp2​+α2p12​,=α2(p12​+p22​).​
(10)

Both have feasible directions p2≥0p_2\ge0p2​≥0. For f1f_1f1​, directions with p2>0p_2>0p2​>0 already increase the objective through the linear term. The exact tested arrow (0,1)T(0,1)^T(0,1)T is vertical and gives increase α\alphaα. Critical directions are p2=0p_2=0p2​=0, where the linear term vanishes and curvature controls the comparison. For f2f_2f2​, the gradient is zero, so every feasible direction is critical and needs the second-order comparison. This characterizes each whole cone, rather than drawing a conclusion from a single tested vector.

Kinematic Interpretation via Example¶

On the positive domain x1,x2>0x_1,x_2>0x1​,x2​>0, consider the following two-dimensional optimization problem:

min⁡x1,x2f(x):=x12−4x1+32x22−7x2+x1x2+9−ln(x1)−ln(x2)s.t.g(x):=4−x1x2≤0h(x):=2x1−x2=0\begin{align} \min_{x_1,x_2} \quad & f(\mathbf{x}) := x_1^2 - 4 x_1 + \frac{3}{2} x_2^2 -7x_2 + x_1 x_2 + 9 - \mathrm{ln}(x_1) - \mathrm{ln}(x_2) \\ \mathrm{s.t.} \quad & g(\mathbf{x}) := 4 - x_1 x_2 \leq 0 \\ & h(\mathbf{x}) := 2 x_1 - x_2 = 0 \end{align}x1​,x2​min​s.t.​f(x):=x12​−4x1​+23​x22​−7x2​+x1​x2​+9−ln(x1​)−ln(x2​)g(x):=4−x1​x2​≤0h(x):=2x1​−x2​=0​​
(11)

The solver implementation below also uses numerical upper bounds x1,x2≤100x_1,x_2\le100x1​,x2​≤100. They are inactive at all three reported solutions and do not change these optima. The logarithms require strictly positive evaluations; zero is not in the mathematical domain even though the numerical lower bounds are written as zero.

Define Function for Visualization¶

## Objective function
def f(x):
    """Evaluate the two-variable objective function."""
    return (
        x[0] ** 2
        - 4 * x[0]
        + 1.5 * x[1] ** 2
        - 7 * x[1]
        + x[0] * x[1]
        + 9
        - np.log(x[0])
        - np.log(x[1])
    )


## Gradient of objective f(x)
def df(x):
    """Evaluate the objective gradient."""
    return np.array((2 * x[0] - 4 + x[1] - 1 / x[0], 3 * x[1] - 7 + x[0] - 1 / x[1]))


## Gradient of inequality constraint g(x)
def dg(x):
    """Evaluate the inequality-constraint gradient."""
    return np.array((-x[1], -x[0]))


## Gradient of equality constraint h(x)
def dh(x):
    """Evaluate the equality-constraint gradient."""
    return np.array([2, -1])

Define function to solve optimization problem with Pyomo¶

def solve_opt(consider_g, consider_h):
    """Solve the example with the selected constraints enabled."""

    ## Create concrete Pyomo model
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()

    ## Declare variables with initial values
    m.x1 = pyo.Var(bounds=(0, 100), initialize=10)
    m.x2 = pyo.Var(bounds=(0, 100), initialize=10)

    ## Declare objective
    m.OBJ = pyo.Objective(
        expr=m.x1**2
        - 4 * m.x1
        + 1.5 * m.x2**2
        - 7 * m.x2
        + m.x1 * m.x2
        + 9
        - pyo.log(m.x1)
        - pyo.log(m.x2),
        sense=pyo.minimize,
    )

    if consider_g:
        ## Add inequality constraint
        m.con1 = pyo.Constraint(expr=4 - m.x1 * m.x2 <= 0)

    if consider_h:
        ## Add equality constraint
        m.con2 = pyo.Constraint(expr=2 * m.x1 - m.x2 == 0)

    ## Specify IPOPT as solver
    solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")

    ## Solve the model
    results = solver.solve(m, tee=True)
    assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(results), (
        f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "
        f"termination={results.solver.termination_condition}"
    )

    ## Return the solution
    return [pyo.value(m.x1), pyo.value(m.x2)]

Three constraint cases¶

The three solves below feed the shared prepared figure after Take 3. The complete visualization, plotting implementation and archived results have one source in this notebook.

Take 1: Unconstrained¶

kkt_solutions = {}
xsln = solve_opt(False, False)
kkt_solutions["unconstrained"] = list(xsln)
print("Primal point:", np.asarray(xsln))
print("Objective:", f(xsln))

Numerical illustration¶

Hatching marks the inequality-feasible side, g(x)≤0g(\mathbf x)\le0g(x)≤0, above the hyperbola. In the third panel the equality also applies, so feasible points lie on the part of the dash-dot line above that boundary.

# Extract the already-computed notebook results; no additional solves.
x1_grid = np.linspace(0.4, 4.0, 200)
x2_grid = np.linspace(0.4, 5.0, 200)
X_grid, Y_grid = np.meshgrid(x1_grid, x2_grid)
results = {
    "grid": {"x1": x1_grid.tolist(), "x2": x2_grid.tolist(),
             "objective": f((X_grid, Y_grid)).tolist()},
    "panels": [
        {"case": name, "solution": kkt_solutions[name],
         "objective": float(f(kkt_solutions[name])),
         "gradient_f": df(kkt_solutions[name]).tolist(),
         "gradient_g": dg(kkt_solutions[name]).tolist(),
         "gradient_h": dh(kkt_solutions[name]).tolist()}
        for name in ["unconstrained", "inequality", "both"]
    ],
}
helper.save_results(
    "kkt-geometry", results,
    notebook="notebooks/7-dev/Local-Optimality.ipynb",
    source_tag=None,
    source_cells=[("notebooks/7-dev/Local-Optimality.ipynb", tag) for tag in
                  ["results:kkt-log-model", "results:kkt-log-functions", "results:kkt-unconstrained",
                   "results:kkt-inequality", "results:kkt-both"]],
    description="Three canonical Ipopt solutions, objective grid and gradients for the shared KKT geometry.",
    solver="ipopt", quiet=True,
)

# The sole shared plotting implementation; archived data are supplied as results.
# Hatch constants follow figures/plots/_house.py; literal values work on Colab.
HATCH_CYCLE = ("//",)
SHADE_ALPHA = 0.18

X1LO, X1HI = 0.4, 4.0
X2LO, X2HI = 0.4, 5.0

# One scale for every gradient arrow. Uniform on purpose: the notebook's own
# discussion cell asks why the arrows are not the same length, and the answer
# (the multipliers, not the drawing) only works if the drawing is honest.
SCALE = 0.35


def _contours(ax):
    X, Y = np.meshgrid(results["grid"]["x1"], results["grid"]["x2"])
    Z = np.asarray(results["grid"]["objective"])
    ax.contour(X, Y, Z, levels=np.arange(-1.0, 12.0, 1.0), colors="0.65", linewidths=0.8)
    ax.set_xlim(X1LO, X1HI)
    ax.set_ylim(X2LO, X2HI)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
    ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")


def _arrow(ax, base, vec, label, scale=1.0, offset=(0.1, 0.1), **kwargs):
    """One gradient, drawn AND named. The name is the greyscale-safe identity."""
    kwargs.setdefault("width", 0.045)
    kwargs.setdefault("length_includes_head", True)
    tip = base + scale * vec
    ax.arrow(base[0], base[1], scale * vec[0], scale * vec[1], zorder=5, **kwargs)
    ax.annotate(
        label,
        xy=(tip[0] + offset[0], tip[1] + offset[1]),
        fontsize=14,
        zorder=6,
        bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=1.0),
    )


def make_figure():
    x_a, x_b, x_c = [np.asarray(p["solution"]) for p in results["panels"]]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.9))
    x1 = np.linspace(X1LO, X1HI, 200)

    for ax in axes:
        _contours(ax)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("$x_2$")

    # --- Panel 1: unconstrained -------------------------------------------
    axes[0].plot(*x_a, marker="*", markersize=18, color="black", linestyle="none")
    axes[0].set_title("1. unconstrained", fontsize=14)

    # --- Panels 2 and 3 share the inequality -------------------------------
    for ax in axes[1:]:
        g_boundary = 4.0 / x1
        ax.plot(x1, g_boundary, color="#0072B2", linestyle="--", linewidth=2.5)
        # Feasible inequality side: x1*x2 >= 4, above the hyperbola.
        ax.fill_between(
            x1,
            np.clip(g_boundary, X2LO, X2HI),
            X2HI,
            facecolor=(0.337, 0.706, 0.914, SHADE_ALPHA),
            hatch=HATCH_CYCLE[0],
            edgecolor=plt.rcParams["hatch.color"],
            linewidth=0.0,
            zorder=0,
        )
        ax.annotate(
            ("feasible" if ax is axes[1] else r"$g\leq0$"),
            xy=((2.15, 4.35) if ax is axes[1] else (2.75, 3.4)),
            fontsize=13,
            bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=1.0),
        )

    axes[1].plot(*x_b, marker="*", markersize=18, color="black", linestyle="none")
    axes[1].set_title(r"2. add $g(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$", fontsize=14)
    _arrow(axes[1], x_b, np.asarray(results["panels"][1]["gradient_f"]), r"$\nabla f$", scale=SCALE, color="black")
    _arrow(
        axes[1],
        x_b,
        np.asarray(results["panels"][1]["gradient_g"]),
        r"$\nabla g$",
        scale=SCALE,
        color="#0072B2",
        offset=(-0.15, -0.42),
    )

    # --- Panel 3: the full KKT picture -------------------------------------
    axes[2].plot(x1, 2 * x1, color="#E69F00", linestyle="-.", linewidth=2.5)
    axes[2].annotate(
        "$h(\\mathbf{x}) = 0$",
        xy=(2.12,4.24),
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->",color="black",lw=.8),
        xytext=(2.4,4.55),
        fontsize=13,
        bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=1.0),
    )
    axes[2].plot(*x_c, marker="*", markersize=18, color="black", linestyle="none")
    axes[2].set_title(r"3. add $h(\mathbf{x}) = 0$", fontsize=14)
    _arrow(axes[2], x_c, np.asarray(results["panels"][2]["gradient_f"]), r"$\nabla f$", scale=SCALE, color="black")
    _arrow(
        axes[2],
        x_c,
        np.asarray(results["panels"][2]["gradient_g"]),
        r"$\nabla g$",
        scale=SCALE,
        color="#0072B2",
        offset=(0.16, -0.40),
    )
    _arrow(
        axes[2],
        x_c,
        np.asarray(results["panels"][2]["gradient_h"]),
        r"$\nabla h$",
        scale=SCALE,
        color="#E69F00",
        offset=(0.08, -0.32),
    )

    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

fig = make_figure()
helper.save_figure(fig, "kkt-geometry", quiet=True)

Discussion¶

Why are the gradient vectors not the same length? I thought the forces were balanced...

Analysis without Constraints¶

For the unconstrained problem, stationarity requires

∇f(x∗)=[2x1−4+x2−1/x13x2−7+x1−1/x2]x=x∗=0.\nabla f(\mathbf{x}^*) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x_1-4+x_2-1/x_1 \\ 3x_2-7+x_1-1/x_2 \end{bmatrix}_{\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^*}=\mathbf{0}.∇f(x∗)=[2x1​−4+x2​−1/x1​3x2​−7+x1​−1/x2​​]x=x∗​=0.
(12)

Numerically, x∗=(1.3475, 2.0470)\mathbf{x}^*=(1.3475,\,2.0470)x∗=(1.3475,2.0470) and f(x∗)=−0.8742f(\mathbf{x}^*)=-0.8742f(x∗)=−0.8742. Moreover,

∇2f(x∗)=[2+1/(x1∗)2113+1/(x2∗)2]=[2.5507113.2387]≻0,\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}^*) = \begin{bmatrix} 2+1/(x_1^*)^2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3+1/(x_2^*)^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2.5507 & 1 \\ 1 & 3.2387 \end{bmatrix} \succ 0,∇2f(x∗)=[2+1/(x1∗​)21​13+1/(x2∗​)2​]=[2.55071​13.2387​]≻0,
(13)

so x∗\mathbf{x}^*x∗ is a strict local minimizer.

Analysis with Constraints¶

KKT system and exact certificate¶

For the constrained problem, define

L(x,u,v)=f(x)+u g(x)+v h(x).\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x},u,v)=f(\mathbf{x})+u\,g(\mathbf{x})+v\,h(\mathbf{x}).L(x,u,v)=f(x)+ug(x)+vh(x).
(14)

The concrete KKT system is

2x1−4+x2−1/x1−ux2+2v=0,3x2−7+x1−1/x2−ux1−v=0,4−x1x2≤0,2x1−x2=0,u≥0,u(4−x1x2)=0,\begin{aligned} 2x_1-4+x_2-1/x_1-u x_2+2v&=0,\\ 3x_2-7+x_1-1/x_2-u x_1-v&=0,\\ 4-x_1x_2&\le0,\qquad 2x_1-x_2=0,\\ u&\ge0,\qquad u(4-x_1x_2)=0, \end{aligned}2x1​−4+x2​−1/x1​−ux2​+2v3x2​−7+x1​−1/x2​−ux1​−v4−x1​x2​u​=0,=0,≤0,2x1​−x2​=0,≥0,u(4−x1​x2​)=0,​
(15)

with x1,x2>0x_1,x_2>0x1​,x2​>0 and v∈Rv\in\mathbb Rv∈R. Products and reciprocals make the stationarity equations nonlinear. Complementarity supplies separate active-state branches, while domain, primal feasibility and multiplier signs remain mandatory checks on every root.

The exact point is (2,22)T(\sqrt2,2\sqrt2)^T(2​,22​)T. Solving the KKT conditions gives the rounded values

x∗=(1.4142, 2.8284),u∗=1.068,v∗=1.0355,\mathbf{x}^*=(1.4142,\,2.8284),\qquad u^*=1.068,\qquad v^*=1.0355,x∗=(1.4142,2.8284),u∗=1.068,v∗=1.0355,
(16)

with g(x∗)=0g(\mathbf{x}^*)=0g(x∗)=0, h(x∗)=0h(\mathbf{x}^*)=0h(x∗)=0, and f(x∗)=0.1579f(\mathbf{x}^*)=0.1579f(x∗)=0.1579. The Lagrangian Hessian is

∇xx2L(x∗,u∗,v∗)=[2+1/(x1∗)21−u∗1−u∗3+1/(x2∗)2]=[2.5−0.068−0.0683.125].\nabla^2_{\mathbf{xx}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}^*,u^*,v^*)= \begin{bmatrix} 2+1/(x_1^*)^2 & 1-u^* \\ 1-u^* & 3+1/(x_2^*)^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2.5 & -0.068 \\ -0.068 & 3.125 \end{bmatrix}.∇xx2​L(x∗,u∗,v∗)=[2+1/(x1∗​)21−u∗​1−u∗3+1/(x2∗​)2​]=[2.5−0.068​−0.0683.125​].
(17)

The exact multipliers are u∗=(17−92)/4>0u^*=(17-9\sqrt2)/4>0u∗=(17−92​)/4>0 and v∗=(5/2)(2−1)v^*=(5/2)(\sqrt2-1)v∗=(5/2)(2​−1). The active inequality and equality gradients are independent. Since the inequality multiplier is positive, a critical direction must be tangent to both constraints; the critical cone is {0}\{0\}{0}, so the second-order sufficient condition is satisfied vacuously. Feasible motion still exists: p=(1,2)T\mathbf p=(1,2)^Tp=(1,2)T is tangent to the equality and enters the inequality interior, but raises the objective to first order.

This particular example also admits a global certificate. On its positive log domain, 4−x1x2≤04-x_1x_2\le04−x1​x2​≤0 is equivalent to 4/x1−x2≤04/x_1-x_2\le04/x1​−x2​≤0, a convex inequality; its second derivative in x1x_1x1​ is 8/x13>08/x_1^3>08/x13​>0. The equality is affine, and the objective Hessian is positive definite throughout the domain: its diagonal entries exceed 2 and 3, with off-diagonal entry 1, so its determinant exceeds 5. The problem therefore has a convex feasible set and a strictly convex objective even though the original product constraint function is not convex. The local minimum is the unique global minimum. This illustrates the representation distinction in Convexity Revisited, rather than applying a failed structural test as a converse.

Sources: Biegler (2010), Eqs. (4.16)–(4.24), p.72; Theorem 4.3, p.65, and Theorem 4.18, p.81. The equivalent-constraint/global certificate and exact multipliers are independently derived from the displayed model. Objective-value source correction: the displayed model has constant +9, yielding approximately -0.874224 without constraints and 0.157862 with both constraints. The book’s -2.8742 and -1.8421 are two units lower and correspond to replacing that constant by +7. The additive constant changes values but not gradients, minimizers, multipliers or curvature. We keep the displayed +9 model and its independently evaluated values.

Active-branch and Hessian details for this same model¶

If the equality is retained but the inequality is assumed slack, set u=0u=0u=0 and x2=2x1x_2=2x_1x2​=2x1​. The restricted objective is

f(x1,2x1)=9x12−18x1+9−ln⁡2−2ln⁡x1.f(x_1,2x_1)=9x_1^2-18x_1+9-\ln2-2\ln x_1.f(x1​,2x1​)=9x12​−18x1​+9−ln2−2lnx1​.
(18)

Stationarity gives 18x1−18−2/x1=018x_1-18-2/x_1=018x1​−18−2/x1​=0, or 9x12−9x1−1=09x_1^2-9x_1-1=09x12​−9x1​−1=0. Its positive root is (9+117)/18≈1.100925(9+\sqrt{117})/18\approx1.100925(9+117​)/18≈1.100925, with x2≈2.201850x_2\approx2.201850x2​≈2.201850. But g=4−2x12≈1.575927>0g=4-2x_1^2\approx1.575927>0g=4−2x12​≈1.575927>0, so this branch is infeasible. The active branch instead enforces 4−2x12=04-2x_1^2=04−2x12​=0, and the positive domain selects the exact point derived above. A root is accepted only after domain, primal feasibility, multiplier sign and complementarity checks.

The Lagrangian Hessian is a sum of scalar-component Hessians,

∇xx2L=∇2f+u∇2g+v∇2h=[2+1/x121−u1−u3+1/x22].\nabla^2_{xx}L=\nabla^2f+u\nabla^2g+v\nabla^2h =\begin{bmatrix}2+1/x_1^2&1-u\\1-u&3+1/x_2^2\end{bmatrix}.∇xx2​L=∇2f+u∇2g+v∇2h=[2+1/x12​1−u​1−u3+1/x22​​].
(19)

At the exact constrained point, the diagonal entries are 2.5 and 3.125, and the off-diagonal is 1−u∗=(92−13)/4≈−0.0680191-u^*=(9\sqrt2-13)/4\approx-0.0680191−u∗=(92​−13)/4≈−0.068019. Biegler Eq.(4.24) p.72 prints a positive off-diagonal. The errata fixes the diagonal signs but leaves that further sign error. The critical-direction matrix

[−22−22−1]\begin{bmatrix}-2\sqrt2&-\sqrt2\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}[−22​2​−2​−1​]
(20)

has determinant 424\sqrt242​, so its null space is zero. It describes directions tangent to the equality and the positively weighted active inequality. It does not describe every feasible direction: (1,2)T(1,2)^T(1,2)T is an inward feasible rail direction and increases the objective to first order.

Printed orientation discrepancy. Biegler Eq.(4.9) p.70 uses transposed vector-constraint gradients, while Eqs.(4.17)–(4.18) p.72 use columns for the same stationarity components. The course consistently defines Jg\mathbf J_gJg​ with constraint rows (r×nr\times nr×n), so Jgp\mathbf J_g\mathbf pJg​p is a constraint-change vector and JgTu\mathbf J_g^T\mathbf uJgT​u is an nnn-component gradient contribution. A single scalar-constraint gradient is a column. This resolves the dimensions without adopting two definitions of the same symbol.

Sources: Biegler Eqs.(4.13), (4.16)–(4.25), pp.71–72, with the displayed positive-domain substitutions and exact derivatives independently checked. The complete multiplier-sensitivity and strong/weak reference is Analysis of KKT Conditions.

For a complete directional interpretation, the equality tangent condition is 2p1−p2=02p_1-p_2=02p1​−p2​=0, so every candidate tangent is p=t(1,2)T\mathbf p=t(1,2)^Tp=t(1,2)T. The active inequality gives ∇gTp=−42 t≤0\nabla g^T\mathbf p=-4\sqrt2\,t\le0∇gTp=−42​t≤0, hence t≥0t\ge0t≥0. Stationarity then gives ∇fTp=42 u∗t\nabla f^T\mathbf p=4\sqrt2\,u^*t∇fTp=42​u∗t. Since u∗>0u^*>0u∗>0, only t=0t=0t=0 has zero first-order objective change: the critical cone is {0}\{0\}{0}, while nonzero feasible inward directions exist. In the figure the direction-space arrow ends at the actual tested vector (1,2)T(1,2)^T(1,2)T; the decision-space arrow is the step 0.3p0.3\mathbf p0.3p. Hatching marks inequality-feasible points or inward inequality directions, while the rail must still be imposed.
